steps.say: Blunt force is blamed for most renal injuries in practice. Eighty five to ninety percent are counted as blunt in civilian series. Road collisions with falls from height are listed as the leading causes. The kidney is cushioned by fat and ribs yet is decelerated fast. Children are judged more vulnerable with less fat. Direct blows with seatbelt injuries are also included.
steps.tx: **Blunt mechanisms** (blunt trauma from road crash or fall impact) cause **over 85% to 90%** (above eighty five in a hundred) of civilian renal trauma, with motor vehicle collisions and falls the leading etiologies. Rapid deceleration shears the vascular pedicle while direct blows crush parenchyma against ribs. Suspect renal injury with flank bruising, lower rib fractures, or haematuria, because deceleration force hides inside the retroperitoneum.

steps.say: Low grade injuries are managed without any surgery. Grade one is defined as a bruise or small subcapsular haematoma without tear. Grade two is marked by a shallow cortical tear under one cm. The perirenal haematoma is expected to stay non expanding. The collecting system is confirmed as intact. Bed rest with monitoring is prescribed as sufficient.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade I** (contusion or subcapsular haematoma) involves bruising without laceration, while **Grade II** (shallow tear) adds a non expanding perirenal haematoma or cortical laceration **less than 1 cm** (under one centimetre) deep with no collecting system rupture. Both grades heal with bed rest, fluids, and serial haematocrit checks. Repeat imaging only for falling counts or fever, because stable low grades rarely deteriorate.

steps.say: Grade three is staged as a deep parenchymal tear. The laceration is measured at more than one cm into cortex. Urine is not leaked because the collecting system is holding. Bleeding is usually tamponaded inside Gerota fascia. Most cases are still kept away from operation. Observation with strict vitals is ordered as the rule.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade III** (deep cortical tear) means a laceration **greater than 1 cm** (over one centimetre) deep with no urinary extravasation and no collecting system tear. Bleeding tamponades within **Gerota fascia** (kidney envelope), so stable patients stay non operative with bed rest and monitoring. Escalate for transfusion need or expanding haematoma, because containment can fail.

steps.say: Grade four is defined by crossing into the collecting system. Urine is extravasated from a torn pelvis or calyx. Segmental vessels are sometimes bleeding but stay contained. Most stable grade four injuries are steered away from surgery. A ureteral stent with bladder catheter is placed to divert urine. Selective angioembolization is used to stop focal bleeding.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade IV** (collecting system tear) brings **urinary extravasation** (urine leak) from a lacerated pelvis or calyx, with segmental arterial or venous injury or active bleeding contained within Gerota fascia. Stable patients heal with a ureteral stent plus Foley diversion, while contained arterial bleeders go for **selective angioembolization** (targeted vessel block). Operate only for instability or shattered anatomy, because stents plus embolization save kidneys.

vis.alt: Ureteral stent diverting urine past a collecting system tear.
vis.caption: Grade IV leaks: stent plus catheter diversion heals most stable tears. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Grade five is staged as destroying or devascularizing the kidney. The organ is sometimes found completely shattered. Hilar avulsion is defined as tearing the pedicle apart. Main artery or vein thrombosis is proved to kill perfusion. These patients are often received in unstable condition. Emergency exploration with likely nephrectomy is undertaken.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade V** (shattered or devascularized kidney) covers a completely **shattered kidney** (fragmented organ), **hilar avulsion** (torn pedicle), or main renal artery or vein thrombosis that kills perfusion. These injuries present unstable with massive retroperitoneal bleeding. Explore emergently after resuscitation, accepting nephrectomy when reconstruction is impossible, because life outweighs the organ.

steps.say: Stable patients are directed to CT and not to theatre. Multiphasic contrast CT is kept as the gold standard test. The arterial phase is used for mapping active bleeding. The nephrographic phase is read for showing parenchymal tears. Delayed excretory images at ten to fifteen minutes are taken to reveal urine leaks. One missed delayed phase is reported to hide a grade four injury.
steps.tx: **Multiphasic contrast CT** (three phase kidney scan) with arterial, nephrographic, and **delayed excretory phases at 10 to 15 minutes** (ten to fifteen minutes) is the imaging of choice in stable patients. Arterial maps bleeders, nephrographic defines tears, and delayed images catch urinary extravasation that earlier phases miss. Never skip the delayed phase when haematuria or high grade injury is suspected, because leaks declare the grade.

steps.say: Most renal injuries are steered away from the knife. Absolute indications for exploration are drawn narrowly. Persistent instability despite resuscitation is ranked as topping the list. Expanding or pulsatile haematoma is judged to demand control. Grade five vascular avulsion is listed for immediate surgery. Penetrating hilar wounds are usually sent to theatre as well.
steps.tx: **Indications for exploration** (mandatory operation triggers) are persistent **haemodynamic instability** (unresponsive low pressure) despite resuscitation, an expanding or **pulsatile retroperitoneal haematoma** (pulsatile hematoma, throbbing flank mass), and Grade V hilar avulsion. Penetrating hilar injuries usually join this list. Everything stable and contained stays non operative with close monitoring, because unnecessary exploration raises nephrectomy rates.

steps.say: Opening Gerota fascia is feared for releasing the tamponade. Bleeding is restarted the moment pressure is lifted. The main renal artery and vein are clamped first before inspection. Control at the aorta and vena cava is established early. The envelope is then opened and inspected calmly. Early vascular control is proven to cut nephrectomy rates sharply.
steps.tx: **Vascular control** (pedicle clamping first) of the main renal artery and vein at the **aorta and IVC** (great vessels) before opening Gerota fascia keeps the tamponade intact until inflow stops. Opening the envelope first restarts catastrophic bleeding and forces hurried nephrectomy. Dissect the pedicle calmly, clamp, then inspect the kidney, because controlled fields allow repair instead of removal.
